title: Columbus, Conquest and the Columbian Exchange

cards.h: The man who sailed to 'India' and never realised where he was
cards.b:
On 12 October 1492, after about ten weeks at sea, a lookout on the Pinta shouted 'Land!' Christopher Columbus stepped ashore on an island in the Bahamas.

He was sure he had reached the edge of Asia. He died in 1506, still believing it.

Since the Ottomans controlled eastern routes, Europeans wanted a sea route to Asia's spices and silk. Portugal was sailing around Africa. Columbus, from Genoa, proposed going west instead.

He got ships from Spain's queen Isabella and king Ferdinand: the Santa Maria, Pinta and Nina. He had guessed Earth was smaller than it is. Educated people knew it was round, but his critics rightly said the distance was far bigger.

Spain and Portugal agreed in the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) to split the new lands between them. A German map of 1507 first used the name America, after Amerigo Vespucci, who argued it was a new continent.

In 1498 Vasco da Gama reached India round Africa. Two routes, one world.
The historian Alfred Crosby named this the Columbian Exchange in 1972. Potatoes helped Europe's population grow. Horses changed Plains life. But germs were deadly.

The Taino people of the Caribbean were nearly wiped out within decades by disease, forced labour and violence. In the mainland, smallpox killed vast numbers. Estimates of the pre-1492 population and the fall vary widely; many scholars say the Americas lost the majority of their people in the first century or so.

Spanish mines like Potosi (Bolivia) poured silver into the world economy.

Columbus was a brave sailor and a harsh governor. Spanish officials arrested him in 1500 over his rule in Hispaniola. Today many places debate statues and holidays named for him. The debate is about the person, but also about what 1492 started.

Both points are true: the voyage changed history, and it began a catastrophe for many.

cards.h: Did Columbus prove the Earth was round?
cards.b:
Myth: everyone thought it was flat until Columbus.Fact: educated Europeans had known it was round since Greek times. Eratosthenes (about 240 BCE) even estimated its size. Columbus was wrong about the size, and if the Americas had not been there, his ships would likely have run out of food.

Another correction: Norse sailors reached North America around 500 years earlier.

Five things to remember

  1. Columbus landed in the Bahamas on 12 October 1492.
  2. He thought he had reached Asia.
  3. Tordesillas (1494) divided the world between Spain and Portugal.
  4. The Columbian Exchange moved crops, animals and diseases.
  5. Da Gama reached Calicut in 1498.

Think about it

  • Can a voyage be both great and terrible?
  • What would Europe eat without the Americas?
